problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}-5{y}^{′}+6y=0,$ which of the following **cannot** be $y(x)?$
worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}-5\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+6{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +6) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda +6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda -2)(\lambda -3)=0,
$$

and so the solutions of the auxiliary equation  are $\lambda =2$ or $\lambda =3.$

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{2x}$ and ${e}^{3x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $2{e}^{x}$ is not a solution.
